items.title: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
items.excerpt: General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies , and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes. Last year , GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range. Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well. Read full article Comments

items.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
items.excerpt: Nissan provided flights from Washington, DC, to Santa Barbara, California, and accommodation so Ars could drive the Rogue Hybrid. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. Nissan has a new version of its best-selling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested back in February. Most of the hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid. That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiast irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for. items.title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
items.excerpt: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison. Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything , which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals , went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling. Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else. It unifies email + messages + docs + tasks + agents + CRM into a single fast interface with shared team-level memory. Everything in your workspace is @linked and searchable so your team (and your agents) never have to switch tools. # Why Macro We built Macro because we wanted a single operating system for our startup. There are many good software products, and we used them all — Slack, Linear, Notion, HubSpot, and Superhuman — but they don't work together as one system. As we scaled our last venture to ~20 people things started to break: every team got their own tools and the company was held together by MCP and Zapier. The company was not computable. It was chaotic. Macro is a complete redesign of work software from the ground up as a single system. Designed by us in NYC and Toronto, dogfooded by our team of ~15 for two years. Built in SolidJS and Rust for speed and reliability. We're focused on building something that any small company or team at a larger company can use as their "operating system". # Features Macro is composed of 'blocks' designed to be modular, extensible, and work together like Lego. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Prompt Injection Is Just the Start of AI Agent Security (Here's What You Need)
items.excerpt: Learn more about agent security here: https://fandf.co/4i1Qs4u My second brain helps me run my entire business, and that means giving it access to a lot of my systems and data, so I check everything it pulls in and keep its access limited. That works for one agent. A company has agents running across cloud platforms and employee devices, and IT has to know which ones exist, who owns them, and what they can reach. Microsoft is expanding Project Perception, building on Agent 365, to secure AI agents at scale. It gives agents their own identity, scopes their access to the task, and contains them as risk changes, without taking away employees' approved access. Dynamic Permissions gives agents task-specific, time-bound access to supported resources, and separately, risk-based access controls evaluate supported agent actions using current risk and policy. Your team reviews and approves protections before they're enforced. Thanks to Microsoft for working with me on this!

items.title: Let Your AI Agent Do ITS OWN Harness Engineering (Here's How)
items.excerpt: Harness engineering is how we make AI agents better over time: improving the rules, skills and memory around the model every time the agent gets something wrong. items.title: SaaS is dead?
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free. items.title: langchain-ai / deepagents
items.excerpt: The batteries-included agent harness. Deep Agents is an open source agent harness — an opinionated agent that runs out of the box. Extend, override, or replace any piece. **Principles:** - **Opinionated** — defaults tuned for long-horizon, multi-step work - **Extensible** — override or replace any piece without forking - **Model-agnostic** — works with any LLM that supports tool calling: frontier, open-weight, or local - **Production-ready** — built on LangGraph (streaming, persistence, checkpointing) with first-class tracing, evaluation, and deployment via LangSmith **Features include:** - **Sub-agents** — delegate tasks to agents with isolated context windows - **Filesystem** — read, write, edit, or search over pluggable local, sandboxed, or remote backends - **Context management** — summarize long threads and offload tool outputs to disk - **Shell access** — run commands in your sandbox of choice - **Persistent memory** — pluggable state and store backends for cross-session recall - **Human-in-the-loop** — approve, edit, or reject tool calls before they run - **Skills** — reusable behaviors the agent can load on demand - **Tools** — bring your own functions or any MCP server Deep Agents is available as a JavaScript/TypeScript library — see [deepagents.js](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagentsjs). > [!NOTE] > **Deep Agents Code** — a pre-built coding agent in your terminal, similar to Claude Code or Cursor, powered by any LLM. items.title: How to Make AI Write Better Solana Code
items.excerpt: AI coding tools can bring the wrong assumptions to Solana. Josh Siegel from Jump Crypto shows how to give Claude and Codex the context they need to write better Solana code. Josh walks through his core prompt, Solana security checklists, test-driven development, and compute unit benchmarks. He then breaks down an oracle update optimization that reduced compute usage from 34,329 to 293 CU for a single instruction. Follow six steps: give AI Solana-specific context, prototype the logic and prepare test data, test correctness and coverage, benchmark compute units, protect your tests, and review code with another AI agent. The case study then shows how Josh applies these ideas to a real optimization problem.

items.title: Lessons From Red-teaming Auto-review, OpenAI's Blocking Monitor
items.excerpt: This work was done by Giovanni Occhipinti, as part of the ERA fellowship and mentored by Monika Jotautaitė (Apollo Research). Summary We red-teamed synchronous control measures in Codex, with a focus on its blocking monitor Auto-review . Our campaign directly analyzed the Codex codebase, searching for exploits that are enabled by the scaffold itself, both against the models used as monitors and other measures such as the Codex sandbox, protections, and deny rules. We found 11 attacks that a misaligned agent could use to defeat the Codex sandbox and Auto-review, executing arbitrary malicious code. Our taxonomy groups the attacks into three vectors: (1) misconfigurations that create coverage gaps in which actions are controlled, such as writes to sensitive targets; (2) fooling the monitor through injections, truncated evidence, or deceptive framing; (3) hybrid attacks that combine the first two vectors, often relying on timing exploits, where actions get approved based on stale content that can be modified before execution. We shared our results and recommendations with OpenAI, who fixed several of the vulnerabilities we found. We believe that these recommendations can apply to future control protocols, suggesting durable design principles: (1) never grant trust to broad code loaders (e.g., pytest); (2) find and close coverage gaps, which often consist of trusted and privileged components (e.g., oversight settings) that the agent can reach without controls; (3) track and mark…

items.title: Unaligned weak models might exploit powerful aligned models
items.excerpt: TL;DR: My previous posts were about strong models delegating to weaker, less aligned ones. The reverse is also dangerous: a swarm of weak, unaligned agents that uses a powerful aligned model as a contractor, without ever telling it what the work is for. Something close to it happened to me, during alignment research. This is the third post in a series, after Memes, not agents, are what will kill us and Making alignment the agent's problem . The $300 bounty from the first post covers this one too (details at the end). In my previous posts I described how a powerful model might delegate work to less aligned, less powerful models and lose control. I now want to talk about the opposite: The risk that a swarm of weak, unaligned agents becomes just smart enough to call a powerful frontier model through API. The world is full of organizations led by evil, stupid people who have morally fine, smart people working for them. This is not a new concept. An agent swarm can easily do the same. It just has to make sure that the aligned frontier models never find out about the consequences of the work they are doing. This has been measured, at least in small setups. Jones, Dragan and Steinhardt showed that combining two models that are each safe on their own gets harmful tasks done much more often than either model alone: the frontier model only gets the harmless-looking parts, and a weak open model does the rest. items.title: Neutral Isn’t Independent: LLM @-invocation
items.excerpt: Consider a situation where multiple news outlets publish similar stories. A reader may model these as independent, and thus strongly update on the information presented. But imagine that the text of the story makes clear that each outlet obtained the story from the same wire service. This suggests the stories may not be as independent as they first appeared, and the reader may have over-updated by modeling them as independent. This is the phenomenon of correlation neglect . Treating the separate stories as independent essentially double-counts the evidence provided by the wire service. Accounting for the correlation in the evidence provided by the stories would reduce the size of the update. It's noteworthy that this can still be an over-update even if each news outlet is unbiased with regard to the coverage subject. Consider the ability to @-invoke an LLM in a conversation. An LLM response that supports one side in the discussion may be modeled as independent evidence for that side. This may be particularly appealing because an LLM may have a lot of the features of a neutral third party weighing in on the discussion. But here again, neutrality or unbiasedness is not the same as independence . The responses LLMs give may be correlated with the responses given by participants in the discussion, and thus may not be fully independent, even if they are unbiased in expectation. items.title: My experiences with the extremes of post-viral illness and brain retraining/mindbody work
items.excerpt: Summary Following an intense viral infection in 2019, I became ill with a mysterious chronic illness, which became progressively worse until mid-2024 when I became partially bedbound with dozens of debilitating symptoms that normal humans only experience in the months/weeks/days leading up to death. Over my years of being ill, I saw over 30 doctors/therapists/health coaches and tried well over 100 different treatments and palliatives. Most of these did nothing or made things worse, or at best provided slight relief. I try to give a sense of what it is like to live with such an illness. In mid-2024 I began a treatment called brain retraining (also known by other names, such as the mindbody approach and mindbody work ; I will use any of these terms throughout the blog post interchangeably), which cannot be explained in such a small space as this summary but which you can think of as a combination of meditation and exposure therapy, and which is widely considered to be a scam in the "complex chronic illness space" (a vague and spread-out space of people who suffer from illnesses such as ME/CFS, MCAS, mold illness, post-viral illness, long COVID, chronic Lyme disease, dysautonomia, POTS, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, and so on, none of which have any widely-agreed-upon cure, and some of which have no widely-agreed-upon diagnosis). items.title: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] In 1999, Professor Clark Elliott is rear-ended by a stranger at a stoplight. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine. Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop. In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday: “At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. I had lost the mysterious initiative that impels us all forward when we walk, and I knew that without brain rest I wouldn’t be getting it back. I considered lying down in the snow.” Over an hour later, Elliott finally manages to cross the parking lot and begins the second phase of his trial: getting into the car. “I’d lost the concept of center. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: YOUNGER with Andie Crosby, President of Calroy Health Sciences
items.excerpt: “Vascular Health Is Foundational Health. Every organ and system in your body relies upon the oxygen, nutrients, and other molecules delivered by your vascular system. Since vascular health underpins overall health, taking care of your vascular health can change your life.” ---Andie Crosby, President of Calroy Health Sciences https://robynbenson.com/podcasts/ Andie Crosby has over 30 years’ marketing and business development experience working with iconic brands such as Nike, Apple, Gap, Proctor & Gamble and magazines such as Rolling Stone, Glamour, and Vanity Fair. In 2010, her personal interest in health and wellness converged with an opportunity to build and lead the first marketing team at The Institute for Functional Medicine (IFM). items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

items.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

items.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens.…

items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. items.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. items.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.excerpt: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems.
